items.md: Calvert Jump & Scavette (2026) ask whether counties that host a state flagship university are more resilient to recessions, measured as a lower local unemployment response than comparable counties without R1 or R2 research universities. They study the dot-com (2001), great (2008) and Covid-19 (2020) recessions separately, each over a three-year post window. The contribution is to move the university-and-local-economy question from long-run growth to cyclical resilience, and to show that the sign is not stable across recessions. The authors propose that flagship towns stabilize demand for non-tradable goods and services through student and staff consumption, building on Howard, Weinstein, and Yang (2022), and that this buffer disappeared when students left campuses in 2020 (pp. 3-6).

items.md: **Design.** Each recession is a separate "treatment" experienced by all counties. The estimand $\tau$ is the difference between two treatments, suffering a recession with versus without a flagship university, not treatment versus no treatment (p. 13). Windows are 1997-2000 pre and 2001-2003 post, 2004-2007 and 2008-2010, 2016-2019 and 2020-2022 (p. 13). The main estimator is synthetic difference-in-differences (Arkhangelsky, Athey, Hirshberg, Imbens, and Wager 2021):

q.exact: Thus, we do not estimate the causal effect of a treatment versus its absence. Instead, we estimate the causal difference between two treatments, i.e., suffering a recession with or without a flagship university.

items.md: **Threats.** No visual parallel-trends check; LAUS county estimates are interdependent within states (pp. 19-20); flagship counties differ in unmeasured ways.

Table 1 lists 50 state flagship universities, 43 classified R1 and seven R2 (Alaska, Idaho, North Dakota, Rhode Island, South Dakota, Vermont, Wyoming) in the 2021 Carnegie classification (p. 7). Enrollment plus employment as a share of home-county population in 2019 ranges from 2 percent (University of Hawaii at Manoa) to 78 percent (University of South Dakota, Clay County) (p. 10). Only 14 flagship counties carry rural-urban code 1; most are 2 or 3 (p. 10). The authors argue flagships were sited for land availability or in state capitals, not local demand, and sit in small to medium cities (pp. 7-8). The panel is annual, 1997-2022; mean flagship-county unemployment was one to two percentage points below controls through 2010 and converged to under one point by 2020 (p. 11). Appendix B regressions use about 20,195, 20,153 and 20,192 county-year observations for the three recessions (pp. 39-40). The number of treated and control counties in the SDiD estimation is not reported in this version.

items.md: **SDiD estimates.** The 2001 effect is a small, insignificant resiliency effect (about -0.1 percentage point, p. 15). The 2008 effect is "more than 0.5 percentage point lower" unemployment, large and significant; the 2020 effect is "almost equal and opposite in magnitude" (p. 14; also pp. 3, 26). Point estimates and intervals are shown only in Figure 3, so exact values and standard errors are not reported in this version.

q.exact: Specifically, flagship uni- versities appear to provide a small positive but insignificant resiliency effect for their host counties during the 2001 recession, a positive resiliency effect during the 2008 recession, and a negative resiliency effect during the 2020 recession.

items.md: **Sectoral employment.** For 2001 the log-employment effects are small or insignificant; for 2008 they are qualitatively similar but about twice as large across industries; in 2020 flagship counties saw large, significant falls in leisure and hospitality employment (pp. 18-19).

q.exact: The effects are qualitatively similar over the 2008 recession window but about twice as large in magnitude. In other words, employment loss in counties with flagship universities was considerably lower than in counties without flagship universities over the 2008 recession, across a range of industries that vary in the tradeability of their output.

The authors read this as local students returning home driving the negative 2020 result.

items.md: **Identification.** The design is clever but the estimand is relative, a flagship county's recession response minus other counties' response, so "effect of a university" is shorthand for everything correlated with hosting a flagship. Flagships are often in state capitals or college towns with heavy education, health and public-sector shares, and the paper does not separate university presence from that industry mix (the Introduction notes that industry mix predicts recession sensitivity, p. 3). SDiD removes pre-trend differences by construction, so there is no pre-trend test; the authors say as much (p. 16). Weights are far more extreme in 2001 and 2020 than 2008 (Appendix A), so the sign reversal and the 2008 result rest on different amounts of reweighting.

**Mechanism.** The consumption story is consistent with the pattern but not isolated. County consumption data are unavailable (p. 17); the sector regressions show lower leisure and hospitality employment in 2020 but cannot separate student spending from the university's own employment, and the 2001 null is also read as supporting the story. In Table B3 the scale term alone is positive and only marginally significant (0.00638, p-value 0.093), and turns negative once local-student share is added.

**Internal consistency.** Section 4.1 uses four pre-years (1997-2000, p. 13), but Appendix C describes "three year" pre and post windows (p. 42). The raw 2001 gap of 0.3 points is larger than the SDiD estimate of about -0.1. Bootstrap uses only 100 replications and no standard errors are tabulated.
**Selection of examples.** Kentucky and West Virginia are chosen because they are clean (p. 22).

**Transfer to 2-year college openings.** This is not an opening design: the treated colleges are long established, and the outcome is cyclical unemployment, not firms, industry mix or patents. The SDiD-with-composite-treatment template and the within-state synthetic control donor pool are usable for single-county openings, and the CBP sector-employment approach could give industry-mix outcomes. Community colleges draw mostly local commuters, and Table B3 suggests the local-student share is what flips the sign, so the consumption channel here should be weaker or different.
County-level consumption data to test the non-tradable demand mechanism directly (p. 17).
Whether effects differ by university size, student origin and tuition-paying status beyond the Appendix B regressions.
Effects of distance learning and college closures on future resilience (pp. 23-24).
Resilience to other shock types ("varieties of recessions", p. 14).
Not reported in this version: numeric SDiD estimates and standard errors, counts of treated and control counties, and bootstrap diagnostics.

For regional policy, the paper suggests anchor institutions can cushion consumption-driven downturns but are not a general hedge: the same institution amplified the 2020 shock. The authors conclude that establishing educational institutions or regional offshoots is likely to improve resilience to consumption-based recessions (p. 26), a stronger conclusion than a design on existing flagships supports. For research on new colleges, the useful lessons are to model composite treatments transparently, to report numeric estimates and the weight distributions, and to test mechanisms with sector employment. Future work should use new openings as the treatment, add firm, industry and patent outcomes, and check whether community colleges, with more local commuter students, produce a smaller cyclical buffer.
